# Contributing to Codjiva

Thanks for your interest in contributing to Codjiva! This guide will help you get started.

## Getting Started

### Prerequisites

- **Rust** (latest stable) with cargo
- **Node.js 22** with npm
- On **Linux**, the system packages Tauri lists, plus `libdbus-1-dev`
- An **agent** (Claude Code, Cursor Agent, ...) or an **API key**, only if you want to run real jobs. The
  tests and the browser version of the interface need neither.

### Setup

```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/aayushch/codjiva.git
cd codjiva

# Install Prettier and ESLint, which format and lint the whole repository
npm ci

# Install the interface's dependencies and start the desktop app
cd ui
npm ci
npx tauri dev
```

To work on the interface without the desktop app, run `npm run dev` in `ui/` and open the address it prints.
The interface then uses a stand-in backend with a made-up workspace, and its jobs need no agent.

### Project Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| `runtime/` | The JavaScript that every artifact carries: the drawing parts, the film engine, the self-test |
| `crates/codjiva-build/` | Turns an agent's source files into one HTML page, after checking them |
| `crates/codjiva-core/` | Workspaces, agents, jobs, artifacts and the write guard. No user interface |
| `ui/src/` | The Svelte 5 interface |
| `ui/src-tauri/` | The Tauri v2 Rust shell |
| `resources/` | Prompts, schemas, agent definitions, fonts and the theme |
| `fixtures/` | Small workspaces for testing, and sessions recorded from real agent runs |
| `scripts/` | Scripts for testing, building, the landing page and formatting |
| `landing/` | The project's web page |

## Development Workflow

1. **Fork** the repository and create a feature branch from `main`.
2. **Make your changes** following the conventions below.
3. **Test** your changes (see Testing section).
4. **Open a pull request** against `main`.

### Branch Naming

Use descriptive branch names:

- `feat/short-description` for features
- `fix/short-description` for bug fixes
- `docs/short-description` for documentation

### Commit Messages

Write clear, concise commit messages:

- Say in a plain sentence what is different for someone who uses the app
- Start with the part of the app when the change belongs to one, followed by a colon
  (`Job panel: drag handle on the bottom edge`, `Landing page: new screenshots`)
- Keep the first line under 72 characters
- Add a blank line and details if needed

## Your responsibility for what you submit

Everything you post to this repository under your name is yours: code, pull request descriptions, bug reports,
comments on issues, and review comments. You are expected to have read it, to understand it, and to be able to
stand behind it when a maintainer asks a follow-up question.

### Using AI tools

You are welcome to use LLMs and coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, or anything else) to help
you write code, investigate a bug, or draft a comment. Codjiva itself is built with them. The tool does not
change who is accountable for the result.

Before you submit anything that an AI tool helped produce:

- **Read it, all of it.** If a sentence or a line of code is there and you cannot say why, remove it or find
  out.
- **Check it against the source.** Verify claims against the actual issue thread, the code, the docs, or the
  linked upstream project. An LLM working from a summary will happily ask questions the issue already answers,
  or describe behaviour the code does not have.
- **Make it yours.** Edit the output into something you would have written. Keep what is correct and relevant,
  cut the rest.
- **Run it.** For code, run the tests and try the change in the app. "The agent said it passes" is not
  verification.

What is not acceptable is pasting an AI tool's output into an issue, review, or pull request without having
done the above. Comments that ask things the thread already states, reviews that flag problems the code does
not have, and PRs whose author cannot explain their own diff cost maintainers more time than they save, and
they erode trust in every other contribution you make.

Maintainers may close, hide, or decline to review contributions that show no sign of having been read by the
person who submitted them. Repeated instances are treated under the [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

If a substantial part of a pull request was generated by a tool, say so in the PR description. It is not a mark
against the PR; it tells the reviewer where to look harder.

## Code Conventions

### Core, builder and shell (Rust)

- **Formatted by rustfmt**, with lines of at most 80 columns
- **No Clippy warnings**: CI runs `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- **No user interface in `codjiva-core`**: the Tauri shell in `ui/src-tauri/` calls it, and so do the tests
- **Errors are sentences for the user**: an `AppError` has a short code and a message that says what went
  wrong in plain words
- **Tests** say in their name what they show, and use a temporary folder as the workspace

### Interface (Svelte)

- **Svelte 5 runes only**: use `$state`, `$derived`, `$effect`, `$props`, never legacy `$:` reactive
  declarations
- **Plain CSS** in `ui/src/styles/`, with the colours of `theme.css`. Check a change in the light and the dark
  theme
- **Formatted by Prettier** and checked by ESLint, with lines of at most 80 columns
- **Every backend call goes through `ui/src/lib/ipc/`**. A new call needs its type in `types.ts`, the real
  call in `tauri.ts` and a stand-in in `mock.ts`, so that the interface still runs in a browser

### Agents, prompts and recorded sessions

- **Agent definitions** are JSON files in `resources/adapters/`. See [adding or changing an
  agent](../docs/AGENTS.md)
- **Prompts** are in `resources/prompts/`. A change to a prompt changes what every later job makes, so say in
  the pull request which jobs you ran with it
- **Recorded sessions** in `fixtures/replay/` are kept exactly as they were recorded. Record a new session
  with `scripts/record-replay.sh` in place of editing one

### General

- Don't introduce abstractions beyond what the task requires
- Don't add speculative error handling for impossible scenarios
- Comments say what the code does now and why, in plain full sentences, for a reader who has never seen the
  file. They do not describe earlier versions of the code

## Testing

### Core, builder and shell

```bash
# Run all Rust tests
cargo test --workspace

# Run the tests of one module of the core
cargo test -p codjiva-core jobs::

# The linter, as CI runs it
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
```

The tests run agents from recorded sessions and keep API keys in memory, so they never start a real agent and
never touch your operating system's credential store.

### Interface

```bash
cd ui

# Type checking and unit tests
npm run check
npm test

# The interface in a real browser, with the stand-in backend
npm run build && npm run e2e
```

### Runtime

```bash
cd runtime/test
npm ci
npm test
```

### The real app

```bash
# The real app window tours itself and reports what it found (macOS)
scripts/selfcheck.sh
```

`scripts/selfcheck.sh` can also run a job from a recorded session, or with a real agent, on a copy of a
fixture. See the comments at the top of the script and `fixtures/README.md`.

### Formatting

```bash
# At the top of the repository
npm run format   # formats every file and wraps comments that are too wide
npm run style    # what CI runs: formatting, lint, and the width of lines
```

## Reporting Issues

- Use the **Bug Report** template for bugs
- Use the **Feature Request** template for enhancements
- Search existing issues first to avoid duplicates
- Report a security problem by email, as the [security policy](SECURITY.md) says, and not as an issue

## Pull Requests

- Fill out the PR template completely
- Link related issues using `Closes #123` or `Fixes #123`
- Keep PRs focused: one feature or fix per PR
- Ensure the tests and `npm run style` pass before requesting review
